newsitem.title: ITALY: Rail boss' graft arrest opens old wounds in Italy.
newsitem.headline: Rail boss' graft arrest opens old wounds in Italy.

text.p: The arrest in a corruption probe of the head of Italy's state railroad triggered a painful flashback on Tuesday to the "Tangentopoli" graft scandal which brought down the country's political and business elite.
Newspapers splashed the arrest of Ferrovie dello Stato (FS) managing director Lorenzo Necci, one of Italy's most prominent public sector executives, across their front pages.
They declared that the nation had not yet put the "Tangentopoli" (Bribesville) affair behind it.
"Tangentopoli Re-explodes," read the banner headline in the respected newspaper Corriere della Sera.
It was referring to thousands of graft investigations, beginning in 1992, which showed that bribes-for-public contracts was business as usual in Italy.
Such illuminaries as former prime minister Bettino Craxi, party leaders and business barons from all sectors were among those caught in the scandal's net.
Two of country's stalwart political parties, the Christian Democrats and Socialists, disbanded as voters made clear they wanted a new era of clean government.
Necci has been overseeing plans to build a high-speed rail network, a multi-billion dollar public works project which will be one of Europe's largest once set into motion.
Magistrates said they would question Necci on Wednesday on suspicion of involvement in a host of crimes including fraud, embezzlement, false accounting, corruption and abuse of office.

Investigators have so far been reticent to reveal specifics about the case. Italian media reports have said judicial sources indicate the probe focuses on suspected bribes paid for lucrative railroad contracts.
Necci was being held in a solitary cell at the jail in La Spezia, northwest Italy, where La Stampa newspaper said he could catch a glimpse of the railroad tracks from his window.
His arrest re-opened old wounds and even Prime Minister Romano Prodi acknowledged it was "worrying for (our) image".

The premier business daily, Il Sole 24 Ore, ran an unusual front-page editorial urging the magistrates who ordered the arrest to move quickly to clarify the situation for the good of Italy's financial well-being and the morale of its citizens.
"(Necci's) arrest deals another big blow to our country's credibility on international markets," it said.
Prodi on Tuesday insisted that his centre-left government, elected in April, was not touched in any way by Necci's arrest and gave assurances that railroad operations would continue.
"The activities of the company will not suffer any interference or any delay," he told reporters in Valencia, Spain, where he was attending an Italian-Spanish summit.
The railroad said on Monday that Necci's duties would be handled by FS chairman Giorgio Crisci and the board.

Necci's arrest was not the first time scandal touched the railroad. In 1988, the entire management board resigned in the so-called "Golden Sheets Affair" which revealed that FS had paid $110 million for nothing more than linen and paper sheets for its sleeper service.

Necci also had previously come under magistrates' scrutiny in connection with the ill-fated Enimont chemicals joint venture of which he was president between 1989 and 1990. He was one of few officers spared indictment.

Magistrates charge that companies spent tens of millions of dollars in bribes to political parties to extricate themsleves from the disastrous venture between agro-chemicals company Montedison and state energy group ENI.
